# rival

## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.rival.0)

BODY
The material exposes five facts and no interpretations: three people share a flat; they argue about chores; they sometimes agree who will do something and later disagree about what that agreement meant; their work schedules change; one friend has begun avoiding the conversations. Everything else — who does more, whether the agreements were spoken or written, why the friend avoids — is not stated, so what follows is a set of conjectures for the asker to check against what they actually know.

The most useful conjecture is that this is not primarily a fairness fight but an ambiguity problem wearing a fairness fight's clothes. An agreement that fixes who but leaves when, to what standard, and under what conditions is only half an agreement; the missing halves get filled in later by each party, sincerely and differently. That would explain the otherwise odd feature of the disputes — that they are about meaning rather than about refusal. Nobody has to be lying for this to recur; the shared record simply never existed.

The second conjecture concerns the schedules. An agreement made under one roster can become unmeetable under another, and where there is no cheap, explicit way to renegotiate, the natural move is silence — which the others will read as defiance. Some of what looks like bad faith may be changed feasibility with no exit route. This also makes the avoidance partly intelligible: if the conversations have become aversive recycling of unwinnable 'what did we mean' disputes, avoiding them is locally rational. But the avoidance could equally be about something else — the friendship, feeling policed, life outside the flat — and the material cannot tell these apart. Both readings, though, point to the same first move: change the format of coordination so it costs less, and ask rather than diagnose.

What the asker can actually do, with two co-decision-makers and one of them withdrawing, is propose, not enforce.

First, stop litigating the past. What an ambiguous agreement meant cannot be reconstructed, only superseded. Say once, at a calm moment, that old disputed agreements are off the table and future ones start fresh — then hold to it, even when relitigating would feel satisfying.

Second, make the next agreements checkable. One shared place — a whiteboard, a shared note, an app — where every agreement names the task, the owner, a deadline, and one line on what 'done' looks like. The point is shared memory, not surveillance, and offering it as a two-week trial lets the others amend or drop it rather than resist it.

Third, build the schedules in. A standing rule: if your schedule changes and you can't do what you claimed, say so by an agreed day and it gets re-dealt. This gives silence somewhere to go besides defiance, and makes the system bend with the very constraint that keeps breaking it.

Fourth, re-approach the avoidant friend at their cost level: ask which format they would actually tolerate — a ten-minute, time-boxed check-in, or messages if that is what they will answer — and offer the trial in that form, framed as making life easier for everyone rather than holding anyone to account. Asking also gathers information about why they avoid, without forcing a diagnosis on them.

Three failure modes deserve naming. A written system among friends can read as distrust, and the record can be repurposed as a charge sheet; the mitigations are the trial framing, a light tone, and an explicit norm that the board is a memory aid, not evidence. Whoever runs the system has acquired a new unrecorded chore — if that is the asker alone, the fix breeds the resentment it was meant to cure, so facilitation should rotate. And most important: if the real issue is that one person in fact does much more, or if the avoidance is about the friendship with chores merely where it surfaces, tidier coordination will not touch it, and the honest move is a different conversation, at a calm moment unrelated to any dispute. This account cannot tell which situation the asker is in; only they can check. The two-week trial doubles as a diagnostic — if a clean slate, a shared record, and a cheap exit route do not reduce the friction, that is evidence the problem was never about the form of the agreements at all.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
